title: What Happens to Your Body When You Exercise?
paragraphs: From the first strides of a run, the body orchestrates a cascade of physiological adjustments. Cardiac output and ventilation rise to meet the sudden demand for oxygen, the arterioles supplying active muscle dilate, and blood is redistributed away from tissues whose functions can be deferred, notably the digestive tract.

Within the muscle fibres, glucose and fatty acids are oxidised to regenerate the energy currency on which contraction depends. The process is strikingly wasteful, with much of the liberated energy dissipated as heat, hence the climb in core temperature and the onset of sweating. As intensity escalates, the fibres lean increasingly on anaerobic metabolism, a rapid but unsustainable source of energy whose by-products accompany the familiar sensations of fatigue.

The brain is by no means a bystander. Exercise augments cerebral perfusion and prompts the release of neurochemicals implicated in mood regulation and stress resilience, and an extensive literature associates habitual activity with improved sleep, sharper executive function and a diminished risk of depression and cognitive decline.

Persisted with over months, training elicits durable adaptations: stroke volume increases, resting heart rate tends to fall, and the musculoskeletal system grows more robust. It is for these reasons that the World Health Organization recommends 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity activity, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity, per week for adults, supplemented by muscle-strengthening work on at least two days.
